ERR-SF-001.mechanical_failure_mode: Degraded upstream O2 sensor element responds slowly to exhaust mixture changes, causing the ECU's closed-loop fuel control to oscillate sluggishly and over-correct, producing erratic trim behaviour without a true rich or lean condition.
ui_remediation_steps: Observe the upstream O2 sensor switching frequency on a scan tool in live data â€” a healthy narrowband sensor should switch > 0.5 Hz (ideally 1â€“2 Hz) at warm idle; a lazy sensor switches < 0.25 Hz or holds mid-voltage.
Check O2 sensor heating circuit â€” if the heater has failed, the sensor runs colder and responds slower; measure heater circuit resistance.
Note: the gas analyser lambda_chem value is the ground truth. If lambda_chem is near 1.0 but the O2 sensor signal is not switching normally, the sensor is suspect.
Replace the upstream O2 sensor.
After replacement, verify switching frequency returns to > 0.5 Hz and fuel trim settles within Â±5 % at warm idle.
Verify the downstream O2 sensor shows normal differential from upstream (confirms catalyst is also healthy).

ERR-SF-002.mechanical_failure_mode: Dead upstream O2 sensor element locks at a fixed output voltage, forcing the ECU into an erroneous fixed-mixture belief and either opening the loop or driving extreme trim adaptation in one direction continuously.
ui_remediation_steps: Observe the upstream O2 sensor voltage in scan tool live data â€” a stuck-rich sensor reads > 0.7 V indefinitely; a stuck-lean sensor reads < 0.2 V indefinitely. No switching occurs.
Verify with the gas analyser: if lambda_chem is normal but the sensor reads stuck, the sensor is confirmed dead.

Check O2 sensor heater circuit â€” a failed heater that never brings the sensor to operating temperature (> 300 Â°C) causes a stuck near-zero voltage from a cold element (cold O2 sensor = lean voltage).
Replace the upstream O2 sensor.
After replacement, verify the sensor begins switching within 30 seconds of engine start (heater brings it to temp quickly on a new sensor).
Recheck fuel trim: should normalise from pegged values within one warm-up cycle.

ERR-SF-003.mechanical_failure_mode: Degraded or failed MAF sensor electronics produce a consistently low airflow signal that does not correspond to actual airflow, causing the ECU to under-fuel and generating a persistent lean condition with associated DTCs.
ui_remediation_steps: Compare the MAF reading (g/s) on the scan tool to the expected value for the engine's idle RPM and displacement â€” typical idle MAF is 2â€“8 g/s per litre of displacement.
Check MAF signal plausibility: if the MAF reads low at idle AND the engine is running lean (trim > +15 %), suspect MAF hardware failure.
Try cleaning the MAF element with dedicated MAF cleaner first â€” if contamination is the cause, trim will recover (see ERR-LC-002).
If cleaning does not restore correct readings, replace the MAF sensor.
After replacement, verify g/s reading matches expected for the engine size and trim returns to Â±5 %.
Check that the new MAF sensor matches the OEM part number â€” aftermarket MAF sensors are a known source of persistent lean codes.

ERR-SF-004.mechanical_failure_mode: MAP sensor internal reference pressure cell shifts from calibration, reporting a biased manifold pressure that corrupts the speed-density fuel calculation and produces a sustained lean or rich mixture depending on drift direction.
ui_remediation_steps: With ignition on, engine off: MAP sensor should read close to barometric pressure (typically 100â€“103 kPa at sea level). Any reading more than 3 kPa off is suspect.
With engine at warm idle: MAP should read 30â€“50 kPa (naturally aspirated idle vacuum). A reading significantly higher or lower at known-good idle conditions confirms drift.
Compare MAP reading to expected vacuum on the fuel trim graph â€” if the MAP is high (under-reading vacuum) when trims are positive, a lean bias from the MAP is confirmed.
Replace the MAP sensor.
After replacement, re-verify key-on reading and idle vacuum reading against known-good values.
Clear adaptive fuel maps and allow the ECU to relearn over one full drive cycle before re-evaluating trims.

ERR-SF-005.mechanical_failure_mode: ECT sensor reports below-operating-temperature coolant regardless of actual engine temperature, permanently preventing ECU closed-loop entry and forcing continuous cold-start enrichment.
ui_remediation_steps: Compare ECT sensor reading on scan tool to actual coolant temperature measured with a contact thermometer at the thermostat housing â€” a > 15 Â°C discrepancy confirms sensor failure.
Check ECT sensor connector for corrosion, water ingress, or pushed-back pin causing a high-resistance fault.

Inspect the thermostat: a thermostat stuck open produces genuinely cold coolant (the sensor reads correctly but the engine never warms up) â€” feel the upper radiator hose. Hot hose at idle = thermostat open (mechanical fault). Cold hose = sensor fault (sensor wrong, engine actually warming normally).
Replace the ECT sensor.
After replacement, verify ECT on scan tool matches contact thermometer within 5 Â°C at operating temperature.
Confirm ECU enters closed-loop (fuel system status = CL) within 5 minutes of reaching normal operating temperature.

ERR-SF-006.mechanical_failure_mode: Contaminated downstream O2 sensor produces a signal pattern that mimics a failed catalyst â€” switching where it should be flat â€” triggering false P0420/P0430 catalyst efficiency DTCs when the catalyst is mechanically intact.
ui_remediation_steps: Verify catalyst efficiency test conditions: coolant temp > 80 Â°C, no misfire DTCs, no fuel trim beyond Â±10 %. If any precondition is broken, fix it first and retest â€” false P0420 is common when fuel trim is skewed.

Compare upstream vs downstream O2 sensor waveforms in live data. A healthy catalyst: downstream is nearly flat (< 0.5 Hz switching). A contaminated downstream sensor: switching at nearly the same frequency as the upstream sensor.
Inspect downstream O2 sensor connector and bung for moisture, oil residue, or coolant seepage â€” these are the common contamination routes.
Substitute a known-good downstream sensor (or a new one) and retest â€” if P0420 does not return over one complete drive cycle, the original sensor was the fault.
If P0420 returns after sensor replacement, the catalyst itself is confirmed defective (ERR-EF-003 boundary â€” out of scope v1).
Clear DTCs after repair and complete one full drive cycle to confirm OBD-II readiness clears.

ERR-SF-007.component_group: Engine Management — Air Metering and Temperature Sensors
ERR-SF-007.mechanical_failure_mode: Air-metering or temperature sensor under-reading, causing the ECU to under-fuel and create true lean combustion. MAF hot-wire contamination (dirt, oil, or debris insulating the sensing element), MAP sensor vacuum leak at the sensor port, or IAT sensor reading artificially high...
ui_remediation_steps: Compare MAF reading at warm idle against the manufacturer specification (typically 2-6 g/s for a 2.0 L engine). A reading consistently below specification with normal idle quality suggests sensor under-read.
Clean the MAF sensor hot-wire with a dedicated MAF cleaner spray — do NOT use brake cleaner, carb cleaner, or any solvent that leaves a residue. Allow to dry completely before re-installing.
Check the MAP sensor vacuum hose for cracks, kinks, or oil contamination — a restricted vacuum signal causes the MAP sensor to under-report manifold pressure, which the ECU interprets as lower load.

Compare IAT reading at cold start against the ambient temperature and ECT reading — all three should agree within a few degrees. An IAT reading that is consistently higher than the other two confirms sensor drift.
If cleaning does not restore correct readings: replace the affected sensor with an OEM-quality replacement. Aftermarket MAF sensors with different calibration curves will cause new fuel-trim errors.
Verify repair: MAF/MAP/IAT readings within specification, fuel trims within +/-10%, gas analyser shows stoichiometric lambda, no lean-mixture DTC returns.

ERR-SF-008.component_group: Engine Management — Temperature and Pressure Sensors
ERR-SF-008.mechanical_failure_mode: Temperature or pressure sensor over-reading, causing the ECU to over-fuel and create true rich combustion. ECT sensor biased cold (stuck at low resistance, reading -40 C on a warm engine), fuel-rail pressure sensor reading high, or MAF over-reading from oil-saturated hot-wire ...
ui_remediation_steps: Compare ECT reading on a scan tool against the mechanical thermostat housing temperature (infrared thermometer) on a fully warmed engine — should agree within 5 C. An ECT reading significantly colder confirms sensor drift.

Measure ECT sensor resistance and compare to the manufacturer's temperature/resistance table — a sensor that reads 2-3 kohm at 90 C should read > 10 kohm at 20 C. A stuck-low resistance (cold reading) forces cold-start enrichment continuously.

Check the fuel-rail pressure sensor reading against a mechanical fuel-pressure gauge — if the sensor reads higher than actual, the ECU reduces injector pulse width thinking pressure is higher, but the error is typically in the opposite direction. A sensor reading low drives the ECU to increase pulse width, creating rich.

Inspect the MAF sensor for oil contamination from an over-oiled aftermarket air filter — the oil film on the hot-wire insulates it, causing the sensor to over-read air mass, which the ECU compensates with more fuel.

Replace the confirmed-faulty sensor with an OEM-quality replacement. After replacement, clear fuel trims and allow the ECU to re-learn. Verify that the replacement sensor reading matches the known-good reference.
Verify repair: sensor readings within specification against known-good references, fuel trims return to within +/-10%, gas analyser shows stoichiometric lambda, no rich-mixture DTC returns.
